# 7.5. R을 이용한 분석 예제

**Exercise:** 사람들의 다이어트 수행이 자존감에 긍정적인 영향을 미치는지를 탐색한 가상 데이터를 사용해 예제를 풀어보자. 이 데이터 셋에는 10명의 실험 참가자들의 다이어트 시작 전부터 세 시점(다이어트 시작 전, 다이어트 시행 3개월 후, 다이어트 시행 6개월 후)까지의 자존감 점수가 반복적으로 측정되었다. 실험 참가자의 각 시점에서의 자존감 점수 평균이 통계적으로 유의미한 차이가 있는지를 분석하기 위해 아래와 같은 영가설과 대안가설이 설정되었다.

- $H_{0}:\mu_{\text{time1}}=\mu_{\text{time2}}=\mu_{\text{time3}}$

- $H_{A}:\text{at least two} \; \mu \;\text{are different}$

## 7.5.1 데이터 로딩 및 기술통계

#### 실습 데이터 다운로드: [self_esteem.csv](../data/self_esteem.csv){download="self_esteem.csv"}

```{r}
###### loading data-set
self_esteem <- read.csv("data/self_esteem.csv")
str(self_esteem)
head(self_esteem)

library(rstatix)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

###### pivoting data frame
se.l <- self_esteem %>%
  gather(key = "time",
         value = "score",
         time.1, time.2, time.3) %>%
  convert_as_factor(id, time)

# se.l <- self_esteem %>%
#   pivot_longer(cols = c(time.1, time.2, time.3),
#                names_to = "time",
#                values_to = "score") %>%
#   mutate_at(vars(id, time), as.factor)

head(se.l)

###### descriptive statistics
library(kableExtra)
se.l %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  get_summary_stats(score, type = "mean_sd") %>%
  kable(digits = 2) %>% kable_paper("hover", full_width=F)

###### eyeball inspection
library(ggpubr)
ggboxplot(se.l, x="time", y="score", add="jitter")
```

## 7.5.2 통계적 가정 검증과 효과크기

### STEP1. Check the normality assumption

- **Detect Outliers**

```{r}
se.l %>%
  identify_outliers(score)
```

- **Visual inspection (Q-Q plot)**

```{r}
library(car)
qqPlot(score ~ time, data=se.l, layout=c(1,3))
```

- **Test statistics**

```{r}
se.l %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  shapiro_test(score) %>%
  kbl() %>% kable_styling("hover")
```

### STEP2. Check the sphericity assumption

```{r}
#Mauchly's chi square by prof.bk
mauchly.chi = function(k, n, W) {
  d <- 1 - ((2 * ((k - 1)^2)+(k - 1)+2)/(6*(k - 1)*(n - 1)))
  a <- -(n-1)*d*log(W)
  b <- (k*(k - 1)/2) - 1
  names(a)=c("Mauchly.chi^2")
  names(b)=c("df")
  print(c(a, b))
}

mauchly.chi(3, 10, 0.551)
```

### STEP3. Conduct one-way within ANOVA

```{r}
se.result <- se.l %>% anova_test(dv = score,
                                 wid = id,
                                 within = time)
se.result


library(ez)
se.ez <- ezANOVA(se.l,
                 wid = .(id),
                 dv = .(score),
                 within = .(time),
                 detailed = TRUE,
                 return_aov = TRUE)
se.ez
```

## 7.5.3 사후-검정

### STEP4. Conduct post-hoc

```{r}
se.l %>%
  pairwise_t_test(score ~ time, paired = T, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni") %>%
  kbl(digits = 3) %>%
  kable_paper("hover", full_width = F)


# plot
se.aov <- anova_test(data = se.l, dv = score, 
                     wid = id, within = time)

tb <- get_anova_table(se.aov, correction = "none")

pwc <- se.l %>%
  pairwise_t_test(score ~ time, paired = TRUE, 
                  p.adjust.method = "bonferroni") %>% 
  add_xy_position(x = "time")

bxp <- ggboxplot(se.l, x = "time", y = "score", add = "point",
                 xlab = "Diet Program",
                 ylab = "Self-esteem")

bxp + stat_pvalue_manual(pwc) +
  stat_summary(
    fun.data = function(x)
    data.frame(y=1, label = paste("Mean=", round(mean(x), digits = 2))),
    geom="text", size=4) +
  labs(subtitle = get_test_label(tb, detailed = TRUE), 
       caption = get_pwc_label(pwc))

```

### STEP5. Conduct trend analysis (optional\*)

```{r}
library(emmeans)
model <- aov(formula = se.l$score ~ se.l$time + Error(se.l$id/se.l$time))
em <- emmeans(model, ~time)

trend <- as.data.frame(contr.poly(3))
# trend <- as.data.frame(contr.poly(length(unique(se.l$time))))

limcombs <- contrast(em, list(linear = trend$.L, 
                              quadratic = trend$.Q))
test(limcombs, adjust = "none")

library(gplots)
plotmeans(se.l$score ~ se.l$time, 
          xlab = "Diet Program",
          ylab = "Self-esteem",
          main = "Mean Plot with 95% CI")
```

### STEP6. Report the result of one-way within ANOVA

```{r}
library(kableExtra)
se.l %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  get_summary_stats(score, type="common") %>%
  dplyr::select(c(time, n, mean, sd)) %>%
  rename(" " = time) %>%
  kbl(digits = 3, align = "c",
      caption = "Table1. Descriptive Statistics for the Perceived Self-esteem by Diet Program") %>% 
  kable_paper()


library(apaTables)
apa.ezANOVA.table(se.ez, filename = "tb_onewayw.doc",
                  correction = "none",   # "GG" or "HF"
                  table.number = 2, 
                  table.title = "Result of One-way Within Subject ANOVA")
```

An one-way repeated measures ANOVA was conducted to assess the effect of diet duration on participants' self-esteem scores across three time points (pre-diet, 3 months after diet initiation, and 6 months after diet initiation). The assumptions of normality and sphericity were assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test and Mauchly’s test ($\chi^2(2)=4.77, p =.09$), respectively. The results confirmed that both assumptions were met. Table 1 shows the descriptive statistics of the data.

As the Table 2 indicated, the result demonstrated that there was a statistically significant difference in self-esteem scores across the three time points at 95% confidence level, *F*(2, 18) = 55.47, *p* \< .001, $\eta_G^2$ = .83. In other words, approximately 83% of the variability in self-esteem scores can be attributed to the time elapsed since diet initiation. Additionally, a trend analysis indicated that data were well fit by a significant linear trend, $t(18)=10.46, p<.001$, suggesting that self-esteem scores increased steadily across time.

Post-hoc comparisons using the Bonferroni correction indicated significant increases in self-esteem scores over time. The mean self-esteem score was lowest at the pre-diet stage (*M* = 3.14, *SD* = 0.55), increased significantly after 3 months of dieting (*M* = 4.93, *SD* = 0.86), and reached its highest average at 6 months (*M* = 7.64, *SD* = 1.14). Each of these differences was statistically significant. In summary, participants’ self-esteem scores showed marked improvement over the diet duration, indicating that continued adherence to the diet may have a positive effect on self-esteem over time.
